To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
1) The δ18O of enamel in modern ruminant species is related to their water intake and dietary proportions of C3 and C4 plants.

(1) the aridity index derived using δ18O values in the enamel of ES and EI herbivores can be affected by changes in paleodietary composition, and (2) this effect can lead to underestimation of the aridity index, and thus overestimation of precipitation, if the paleodiet is dominated by grasses in ES taxa.
1) The δ18O value of the enamel of ruminant herbivores reflects evaporation of water from leaves and stems of dicots and not from the water of drinking.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of stable isotope ratios in mammalian tooth enamel as a proxy for ancient aridity.
the use of δ18O values in tooth enamel to infer water deficit in the past.
the potential influence of paleodietary shifts on the aridity index and the need for caution when using it in the absence of dietary screening of the fossil taxa.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
“The aridity index derived by comparing enamel δ18O between ruminants that consume a diet rich in grass and those that consume a diet dominated by leafy dicots is a useful proxy for water deficit.
the δ18O-based aridity index is not a reliable tool for reconstructing ancient water deficit.
the use of the δ18O of mammalian herbivore tooth enamels to infer aridity indices should not be used in cases where the diet of the fossil herbivores is not known.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the aridity index is a useful tool for paleohydrologic reconstruction but requires careful consideration of the paleodietary composition of fossil taxa.
the δ18O of tooth enamel in fossil ungulate herbivores should be interpreted cautiously in paleohydrological reconstructions.
the aridity index derived for East Africa is likely to be an underestimation of water deficit during the Pleistocene.
The main takeaway from our work is that
paleodiet is important to consider in paleo-environmental reconstructions using δ18O of mammalian tooth enamel.
, in the case of ruminants, it is necessary to ensure that the diet of a fossil taxon is consistent with its assumed drinking behavior.

the use of the aridity index derived by comparing the δ18O of fossil ungulates with different water sources (e.g., ruminants versus non-ruminants) is only valid when the diet of fossil taxa is known and consistent with the assumptions of such comparisons.
